Add to Preferred Sources A new lithium dawn is breaking over Mali’s mining industry. Pic: Getty Images
Add to Preferred Sources Mali’s gold potential has attracted some of the world’s leading miners Lithium is now gaining momentum with two mines in production First Lithium is working towards a maiden resource estimate
Mali’s history of mining stretches back centuries to the days of the Mali Empire and its legendary ruler Mansa Musa.
Musa is regarded as one of the world’s richest people to have ever lived, with his fortune built on the empire’s gold and salt trade.
He famously passed through Cairo on a pilgrimage to Mecca in the 14th century, giving away so much gold that it reportedly depressed the metal’s value for years.
Today, gold remains integral to Mali’s economy and mining sector.
Barrick Mining, one of the world’s largest gold producers, operates the Loulo-Gounkoto complex in western Mali.
Canadian heavyweights B2Gold and Allied Gold also churn out the metal in the country.
On the ASX, Africa-focused producer Resolute Mining (ASX:RSG) is targeting between 150,000 ounces and 160,000 ounces of output in 2026 from its Syama mine.
Toubani Resources (ASX:TRE) could be the next ASX gold producer in the nation, with first pour at its Kobada project targeted for next year.
Gold may have put Mali on the map, but lithium is now adding another important dimension to the country’s mining story.
Chinese giant Ganfeng commenced production at its Goulamina mine in late 2024, with UK-listed Kodal Minerals and its Chinese partner Hainan Mining bringing their Bougouni project online last year.
ASX explorer First Lithium (ASX:FL1) is also on the hunt for lithium at its Faraba and Gouna projects.
Previous drilling at Gouna returned a series of notable strikes at the priority Blakala prospect, including 111m at 1.57% Li2O.
The recent renewal of both exploration licences has cleared the way for the company to advance a maiden resource estimate.
West Africa is considered one of the world’s most prospective gold provinces.
Its mineral wealth is underpinned by the West African Craton, a geological terrane often compared with WA’s prolific Yilgarn Craton.
Most of the region’s major gold deposits are associated with Birimian greenstone belts.
These features stretch across several countries, including Mali, and have helped transform Ghana into one of the world’s biggest gold producers and the largest in Africa.
West Africa’s potential has not gone unnoticed by the world’s leading gold miners, with the likes of Newmont Corporation (ASX:NEM) , AngloGold Ashanti and Barrick operating in the region.
In Mali, Barrick’s 80% owned Loulo-Gounkoto complex includes the Yalea and Gara underground mines and the Gounkoto open pit.
The remaining 20% of the operation is owned by the Malian government, which has sought to increase its share of the country’s mineral wealth through reforms to its mining code.
Barrick expects its share of production to total between 260,000 and 290,000 ounces in 2026.
The project hosts about 6.9Moz in reserves and about 11Moz in resources.
B2Gold’s 80%-owned Fekola mine achieved first gold pour in 2017.
It has since served up more than 4Moz, with 390,000-420,000 ounces targeted from the broader Fekola complex in 2026.
Allied Gold is guiding for production of at least 200,000 ounces in 2026 from its majority-owned Sadiola mine. The asset hosts nearly 7Moz in reserves.
Amongst the ASX contingent, Resolute brought its Syama project to life in 2018.
It still contains 3.9Moz in reserves and 9.1Moz in resources.
Elsewhere, Toubani is targeting first production at Kobada in the third quarter of next year.
A recent DFS outlined a 9.2-year operation with annual production of about 162,000 ounces.
The project currently holds a 2.2Moz resource with further exploration potential.
Mali’s lithium-bearing pegmatites have also been attracting investor interest over the past few years.
Ganfeng shipped its first concentrate from Goulamina last June and is now ramping up production.
A planned expansion is targeting annual production capacity of 1Mt lithium concentrate.
The company initially partnered with ASX-listed Leo Lithium in 2021 to advance the project.
It acquired Leo’s remaining 40% stake for about US$343 million in 2025, before the Malian government secured a 35% interest under a revised mining agreement.
Goulamina is regarded as one of the world’s largest hard-rock lithium deposits, with a resource totalling 299Mt at 1.33% Li2O.
Meanwhile, Kodal and Hainan produced first concentrate at Bougouni in February 2025.
The first stage of production entails 125,000 tonnes of concentrate per annum over four years.
A proposed second-stage flotation plant is expected to extend the mine life by more than 10 years and lift output to 230,000 tonnes per annum.
Bougouni holds a resource totalling 31.9Mt at 1.06% Li2O, with further exploration potential.
First Lithium has also identified exploration upside at its Faraba and Gouna tenements, sitting about 50km apart in southern Mali.
Multiple spodumene-bearing pegmatites have been identified across the two projects.
At Gouna, previous drilling delivered a series of significant intercepts along 1.3km of strike of the main pegmatite body at Blakala.
Drilling in 2023 returned 111m at 1.57% Li2O from 33m and 60m at 1.59% Li2O from 39m.
Subsequent results included 41m at 1.91% Li2O from 80m and 37m at 1.79% Li2O from 88m.
The company is now targeting a maiden resource before the end of the year after securing licence renewals for both projects for a further three years.
